explanation: == compares whether two objects have equal values.
is compares whether two references point to the same object.
Equality behaviour can be customised through __eq__(), while identity cannot be customised.
Use is or is not when comparing with None.
Identity comparison is appropriate when checking a specific singleton or sentinel object.
Do not use is for equal strings or numbers because implementation details such as interning can make identity appear inconsistent.
A mutable object can be changed in place, while an immutable object cannot.
Lists and dictionaries are mutable; strings, integers, and tuples are immutable.
Rebinding a name is different from mutating an object: rebinding changes which object the name references.
A shallow copy creates a new outer object but retains references to nested objects.
A deep copy recursively copies nested objects where possible.
Changes to shared nested objects can appear in both the original and a shallow copy.
Passing a function without parentheses passes the function object itself.
Adding parentheses calls the function immediately and passes its return value.
A callback is stored and invoked later when an event or condition occurs.
Functions can be assigned to names and stored in data structures.
Functions can be passed as arguments and returned from other functions.
Functions are objects with attributes and participate in Python's callable protocol.
An iterable can provide an iterator when passed to iter().
An iterator produces one item at a time when passed to next().
Iterators are consumed as they advance, while many iterable containers can create a fresh iterator for each traversal.
A for loop obtains an iterator by calling iter() on the iterable.
It repeatedly calls next() to retrieve values.
The loop ends normally when the iterator raises StopIteration.
Type annotations communicate intended types to readers.
Static analysis tools and editors use annotations to detect likely mistakes and improve assistance.
code_example: def greet(name: str) -> str:\n    return f"Hello, {name}!"

explanation: Annotations document expectations without changing Python's fundamentally dynamic type system.
Python does not normally enforce type annotations at runtime.
Static type checkers examine annotations without executing the program.
Runtime validation requires explicit code or a library designed to perform it.
A context manager controls setup and cleanup around a defined block of work.
code_example: with open("animals.txt") as file:\n    animals = file.read()

explanation: The with statement ensures the context is exited even when the block raises an exception.
Common uses include files, locks, database transactions, temporary resources, and temporary state changes.
__enter__() prepares the context and returns the value optionally bound by as.
__exit__() performs cleanup when execution leaves the with block.
__exit__() receives information about an exception raised inside the block, or three None values after normal completion.
__exit__() can inspect the exception type, value, and traceback.
Returning a truthy value suppresses the exception; returning a false value or None allows it to propagate.
The method may perform cleanup or logging regardless of whether it suppresses the exception.
